summary: Extends WebDAV so clients and servers can specify the datatype of a property, and so the PROPFIND method can return datatype information. It defines an Experimental Protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Properties of a file are normally just text. This experiment lets them say whether they are numbers, dates, or something else.

questions: how to specify property type in webdav
subtitle: Adding datatypes to WebDAV property values so servers can interpret them correctly.

tldr.problem: WebDAV properties are stored as XML elements, which means the server cannot distinguish between a number stored as text and an actual numeric value. Clients and servers have no standard way to communicate a property's intended datatype.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds an optional xsi:type attribute to property elements, borrowing the XML Schema datatype notation. Clients can supply this when setting properties via PROPPATCH, and servers can return it in PROPFIND responses to indicate the type they have stored.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now optimize storage and perform type-aware operations like comparisons and sorting. However, this remains an Experimental protocol with limited adoption.

today: RFC 4316 defines an Experimental protocol. It remains experimental and has seen limited adoption in WebDAV implementations. Servers can implement datatype support independently, but there is no widespread deployment.

sections.title: What WebDAV Properties Need
sections.content:
WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning) lets programs store and retrieve files on servers over HTTP, along with properties attached to those files—metadata like author, revision, or custom attributes. Currently, all property values are stored as XML elements that contain text.

The problem is that a property value of 42 looks identical to the text string 42 when it arrives at the server. A date like 2005-12-15 is indistinguishable from the same characters as plain text. Servers cannot know whether to store a value as a number, boolean, date, or just text, so they cannot optimize storage or perform type-aware operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, WebDAV doesn't tell you if 42 is a number or just text. This makes it hard for servers to store things efficiently or do math with the values.

sections.title: The Datatype Solution
sections.content:
This specification borrows XML Schema datatypes, a standard set of types defined by the W3C. It adds a single attribute, xsi:type, to property elements. When a client sets a property via the PROPPATCH method, it can include an xsi:type attribute naming the datatype—for example, xs:boolean for a true-or-false value, or xs:integer for a whole number.

Servers that understand this extension can parse the value according to the specified type and store it in an optimized format. When a client retrieves the property via PROPFIND, the server can return the same xsi:type attribute so the client knows how to interpret the value.

The datatype information is purely advisory. Clients that do not supply it, and servers that do not recognize it, continue to work; the datatype attribute is simply ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: You add a label like 'number' or 'true-or-false' when you set a property. The server reads that label and stores the value the right way. When you ask for the property back, the server tells you what kind of value it is.

sections.title: The Type Attribute
sections.content:
Type information is represented using the XML attribute xsi:type, which is defined in the XML Schema-Instance namespace (http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance). The value of this attribute is a qualified name referring to one of the built-in XML Schema types, such as xs:boolean, xs:integer, xs:date, or xs:string.

For example, when setting a property called released to the value true with a boolean type, a client sends:

<Z:released xsi:type="xs:boolean">true</Z:released>

Servers may implement any combination of datatypes from the XML Schema recommendation or from custom namespaces. Type information is only required when it adds usable information; properties already defined in the base WebDAV specification and simple text strings do not need a datatype attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The type information is just one XML attribute that names a type like 'boolean' or 'integer'. You add it to the property element, and the server understands what it means.

sections.title: Changes to PROPPATCH and PROPFIND
sections.content:
The PROPPATCH method is used to set properties on a resource. When a client includes an xsi:type attribute on a property element, the server can use this information to validate and parse the value correctly. If the server successfully parses the typed value, it SHOULD return the xsi:type attribute in the response, confirming that it understood the type.

For example, if a client sends a property with xsi:type="xs:boolean" but supplies the invalid value t (not a valid boolean), the server responds with a 422 Unprocessable Entity status and an error message. If the value parses correctly, the server confirms success with a 200 OK and echoes back the type attribute.

The PROPFIND method retrieves properties from a resource. When returning properties, servers that support datatypes now include the xsi:type attribute for any property whose datatype is not the default (xs:string) and is not already defined in the base WebDAV specification. This tells clients the type of each property value.
sections.plainLanguage: When you set a property with a type label, the server checks if the value makes sense for that type. If it does, it says 'OK' and remembers the type. When you ask for the property, the server tells you the type so you know how to use the value.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
This extension maintains compatibility with existing WebDAV clients and servers. Old clients that do not know about datatype handling simply omit the xsi:type attribute when setting properties, and the protocol works as before. Old servers that receive the xsi:type attribute either drop it or store it as part of the property value (depending on their implementation), but they do not indicate successful parsing by returning the type in the response. New clients can detect server support by checking whether the type attribute appears in the PROPFIND response.

Other methods that use the WebDAV multistatus response format, such as REPORT (defined in RFC 3253), SHOULD apply the same datatype extensions for consistency.
sections.plainLanguage: Old programs that don't know about types can ignore the type label and everything still works. New programs can check if the server sent back the type label to see if it understood the type.
